L305@P4: There were also many updates to other libraries:
L306@P4: • Light Charged Particles: New alpha sublibrary,
L307@P4: p,d,t on 7Li and 3He on 3He
L308@P4: • Decay sublibrary: Improved beta intensities for
L309@P4: some fission products; modified K X-ray energies
L310@P4: for selected actinides
L311@P4: • Atomic sublibraries: Minor fixes and reformatting resulting in a update of all three atomic sublibraries
L312@P4: All these changes were performed in an environment
L313@P4: of dramatically improved quality assurance enabled by
L314@P4: computational advances. Much of the ENDF/B workflow
L315@P4: has been automated now. This process started with the
L316@P4: introduction of the GForge collaboration environment installed at the National Nuclear Data Center which includes both revision control, library release management
L317@P4: and bug tracking. GForge has now been connected to
L318@P4: the ADVANCE continuous integration system [25]. ADVANCE runs a battery of physics and format checks on
L319@P4: every changed evaluation of every commit. This checking
L320@P4: with ADVANCE completely automates the traditional
L321@P4: ENDF/B Phase I testing. ADVANCE also benefits from
L322@P4: the code modernization push that led to both the development of the FUDGE and NJOY2016 processing codes.
L323@P4: These processing improvements in turn led to new tests
L324@P4: and identification of issues in various evaluations. The
L325@P4: processing code modernization efforts in the US, Europe
L326@P4: and Asia are in large part a result of the roll out of the
L327@P4: new GNDS formatting option discussed in Section XIII.

L417@P5: measurements not shown, for example, for p−p scattering,
L418@P5: and for n−p capture, are also fit quite well by this analysis,
L419@P5: and they further constrain the results for n− p scattering.
L420@P5: The new analysis preserves the values of the lowenergy n − p scattering lengths, a0 = −23.719(5) fm and
L421@P5: a1 =5.414(1) fm obtained in an earlier analysis that went
L422@P5: up to 30 MeV, which formed the basis for the ENDF/B
L423@P5: VII.1 hydrogen evaluation. The changes from that earlier analysis remain small at higher energies, as shown
L424@P5: in Fig. 5 [10], which plots the ratios of ENDF/B-VIII.0
L425@P5: to ENDF/B-VII.1 for the total cross section and for the
L426@P5: zero-degree proton laboratory differential cross section. A
L427@P5: small change in the thermal capture cross section, from
L428@P5: 332.00 mb to 332.58 mb, now agrees better with one of

L432@P5: This is because the analysis will eventually be extended to
L433@P5: 200 MeV (a preliminary version already exists for energies
L434@P5: up to 100 MeV).

L1431@P41-42: 230.5. REPRESENTATION OF DATA
L1432@P42: The first record of every section contains a ZA number that identifies the specific material.
L1433@P42: ZA variants are also employed to identify projectiles and reaction products. In most cases,
L1434@P42: ZA is constructed by
L1435@P42: ZA = 1000.0 × Z + A,
L1436@P42: where Z is the atomic number and A is the mass number for the material. If the material is
L1437@P42: an element containing two or more naturally occurring isotopes in significant concentrations,
L1438@P42: A is taken to be 0.0. For mixtures, compounds, alloys, or molecules (evaluations using the
L1439@P42: thermal scattering law (TSL) formats in Chapter 7), special ZA numbers between 1 and 99
L1440@P42: can be defined (see Appendix C).
L1441@P42: A material, incident particle (projectile), or reaction product is also characterized by a
L1442@P42: quantity that is proportional to its mass relative to that of the neutron. Typically, these
L1443@P42: quantities are denoted as AWR, AWI, or AWP for a material, projectile, or product, respectively. For example, the symbol AWR is defined as the ratio of the mass of the material to
L1444@P42: that of the neutron.13 Another way to say this is that “all masses are expressed in neutron
L1445@P42: units.” For materials which are mixtures of isotopes, the abundance weighted average mass
L1446@P42: is used.
L1447@P42: 0.5.1.1 Atomic Masses Versus Nuclear Masses
L1448@P42: Mass quantities for materials (AWR for all Z) and “heavy” reaction products (AWP for
L1449@P42: Z > 2) should be expressed in atomic units, i.e., the mass of the electrons should be
L1450@P42: included. Mass quantities for incident particles (AWI) and “light” reaction products (AWP
L1451@P42: for Z ≤ 2) should be expressed in nuclear mass units. For neutrons, this ratio is 1.00000.
L1452@P42: For charged particles likely to appear in ENDF files, see Appendix H.
L1453@P42: 0.5.2 Interpolation Laws
L1454@P42: Many types of ENDF data are given as a table of values on a defined grid with an interpolation law to define the values between the grid points. Simple one-dimensional “graph paper”
L1455@P42: interpolation schemes, a special Gamow interpolation law for charged-particle cross sections, simple Cartesian interpolation for two-dimensional functions, and two non-Cartesian
L1456@P42: schemes for two-dimensional distributions are allowed.
L1457@P42: 0.5.2.1 One-dimensional Interpolation Schemes
L1458@P42: Consider how a simple function y(x), which might be a cross section, σ(E), is represented.
L1459@P42: y(x) is represented by a series of tabulated values, pairs of x and y(x), plus a method for
L1460@P42: interpolating between input values. The pairs are ordered by increasing values of x. There
L1461@P42: will be NP values of the pair, x and y(x) given. The complete region over which x is defined
L1462@P42: is broken into NR interpolation ranges. An interpolation range is defined as a range of the
